questions.question: What is a token?
options: A vocabulary entry: a learned byte sequence, often a word piece with its leading space
questions.explanation: Tokenizers learn chunks of bytes. Common words are one token; rare ones are several.

questions.question: In BPE training, what becomes the next new token?
options: The most frequent adjacent pair of existing tokens in the training text
questions.explanation: Frequent sequences get merged first, so they end up as single tokens.

questions.question: Why can byte-level BPE encode any text, including emoji?
options: It has every emoji in its vocabulary
All 256 bytes are base tokens, so anything unlearned falls back to bytes
questions.explanation: Nothing is ever out of vocabulary; unfamiliar text just costs more tokens.

questions.question: What does pre-tokenization prevent?
options: Merges that cross word boundaries, like learning whole sentences as one token
questions.explanation: Splitting into word-sized chunks first keeps merges inside words.

questions.question: With llama3.2's tokenizer, English prose was 5.2 characters per token and Hindi 1.8. What does that mean for an agent?
options: Hindi conversations fill the context window and cost about 3x as much for the same length
questions.explanation: Token cost per character varies widely by script and content type.

questions.question: A model has an 8,192-token window. System is 600 tokens, tools 900, and you reserve 1,024 for output. How much is left for history?
questions.explanation: 8,192 - 600 - 900 - 1,024 = 5,668. Output must fit in the same window as the input.
